audits.mathematicalReason: A rectangular prism has four edges on each of two opposite rectangular faces and four edges joining corresponding vertices: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Counting these edges falls within cnm_p160's description of rectangular prisms' faces, edges, and vertices.

figureEvidence.fact: The drawing shows two opposite rectangular faces, each bounded by four edges, with four additional edges joining their corresponding corners.

audits.mathematicalReason: A prism with an n-sided base has n edges on each of its two bases and n lateral edges, giving 3n edges altogether. Thus 3n = 21 and n = 7. This directly assesses the edge structure covered by cnm_h105; the relationship does not require the prism to be right.

figureEvidence.fact: The prism has matching upper and lower polygonal bases with corresponding vertices joined by lateral edges. Each depicted base has seven sides.

audits.mathematicalReason: An upright right circular cylinder has rectangular front and left-side views and a circular top view. It is the matching solid among the choices. Selecting a solid from its three views directly matches cnm_p152.

figureEvidence.fact: The views labeled Front and Left are rectangles, while the view labeled Top is a circle.

audits.mathematicalReason: If the unknown leg is x, the Pythagorean theorem gives x² + 5² = 13², so x² = 144. Since a side length is positive, x = 12. Finding a third side from two known sides explicitly matches cnm_174's criteria.

figureEvidence.fact: A right-angle marker is shown between the bottom and vertical sides. The bottom leg is labeled 5, and the opposite slanted side—the hypotenuse—is labeled 13.

audits.mathematicalReason: Angles between the two lines and on opposite sides of the transversal are alternate interior angles. This is a positional definition covered by cnm_066; parallelism is not required to name the angle pair, and no equality of angle measures is needed.

figureEvidence.fact: Transversal c crosses lines a and b. One marked angle lies below a on one side of c, and the other lies above b on the opposite side of c.

audits.mathematicalReason: In three-letter angle notation, the middle letter identifies the vertex. Thus the vertex of ∠AOB is O, the common endpoint of its two rays. This falls directly within cnm_056's angle-concept and notation scope.

figureEvidence.fact: The two angle arms extend from the marked point O toward A and B, and the angle arc is drawn at O.

audits.mathematicalReason: Each right triangle has area (3 × 4)/2 = 6. In the depicted arrangement, the central square has side 4 − 3 = 1. The large square therefore has area 4 × 6 + 1² = 25 square units. The requested addition of component areas directly assesses cnm_p150, with triangle and square area formulas as appropriate support. A general proof of the Pythagorean theorem is not requested.

figureEvidence.fact: Four right triangles partition the outer square around a central small square. Triangle legs labeled 4 and 3 align with neighboring legs so that their difference gives a side of the central square.

audits.mathematicalReason: Option A contains a 2-by-2 block, whose four squares share one grid vertex. Folding without cutting would keep that shared vertex, but only three distinct cube faces can meet at a cube vertex, so A cannot be a cube net. Options B, C, and D can each fold into six distinct cube faces. Judging cube nets is explicitly included in cnm_051's criteria.

figureEvidence.fact: Option A has four squares in the upper row and two squares directly below the leftmost two, creating a 2-by-2 block.
Option B consists of two three-square rows, with the lower row starting directly beneath the rightmost square of the upper row.
Option C has three two-square rows, each shifted one square to the right of the row above, producing an alternating staircase.
Option D has a four-square horizontal strip, with one square attached above and another below the strip's second square from the left.
